title: Book celebrates Nellie Kenyon, writer of stories related to Scopes Monkey Trial - NewsBreak
text: As July marks the 100th anniversary of the famous Scopes Monkey Trial in nearby Dayton, Tennessee, and its focus on teaching evolution, observers have been talking about the parallels with current education-related debates. One aspect that is not the same, however, is the role of women. While female journalists proliferate in media today, when the Scopes Trial was taking place, Nellie Kenyon was a rare female reporter on hand. She was writing trial-related stories for the Chattanooga News in a trend-setting role before going on to a distinguished career with the Tennessean in Nashville and eventual induction into the Tennessee Journalism Hall of Fame. She also has a Knoxville connection — her papers, scrapbooks and photographs from her career are stored in the University of Tennessee’s Betsey B. Creekmore Special Collections. One person who looked through them and wrote a book on her was Tyler Boyd of Athens, who in 2022 penned “Nellie Kenyon: Trailblazing Tennessee Journalist.” While she did not cover the actual trial proceedings — Boyd is not sure why — she did get to write a lot of trial-related stories from Dayton at the time as the first reporter to receive a press pass. Those stories brought her some attention, and today they offer a broader historical and anecdotal view on that famous trial, he said. “Instead of reporting on the actual trial, she was sent over early to see how the town was preparing for it,” Boyd said in a recent phone interview. For example, she talked to the county judge and encouraged him to clean up the then-dirty Rhea County Courthouse for the trial, and she also talked with the jurors. In addition, she interviewed some local businessmen, who had hoped for large crowds and a brief windfall of money. “That didn’t actually happen,” Boyd said. “The local businesspeople were kind of disappointed.” The famous people in this trial that included noted lawyers Clarence Darrow and William Jennings Bryan were also among her interview topics. “She got to talk to a lot of big-time players, and she took (famous reporter H.L.) Mencken to a holy roller (Pentecostal) church,” Boyd added. Her most notable accomplishment related to the trial, he believes, was uncovering the motivation behind it. She learned that some Dayton businesspeople had seen a Chattanooga newspaper article about the American Civil Liberties Union wanting to find someone to test the new state law preventing the teaching of evolution. “She is literally the person who discovered that the whole thing was planned and cooked up in a pharmacy” (to get the town some publicity), he said. Boyd, who has also written a book about his relative Harry T. Burn and his Tennessee General Assembly vote that allowed the passage of the 19th Amendment giving women the right to vote, said the trial brought her some attention. Still, she is not a household name today even in Tennessee, he said, even though her later work included interviewing presidents, baseball player Babe Ruth, gangster Al Capone and Teamsters head Jimmy Hoffa. She also helped expose the Georgia Tann adoption scam. A diminutive woman known as a persistent, straightforward and objective reporter, Kenyon once saw Hoffa in a Cincinnati hotel lobby while covering a trial. He reportedly said to her, “Hello, Nellie dear.” Her reply to him was, “Hello, Jimmy dear.” She grew up in Chattanooga as the daughter of a female society writer for the News, but Kenyon apparently wanted to be a regular news reporter when that was rare. She left for Nashville in 1940 not long after her mother died and after the News was purchased by the Free Press under former Knoxville White Stores owner Dwight McDonald’s brother, Roy. A lifelong single woman, she became a well-known journalist in Nashville covering the federal beat before her retirement in 1970 and death in 1982 at the age of 83. Tennessean publisher John Seigenthaler said at the time of her death that she was honest, accurate and very good at what she did. Boyd said he was able to interview a few people who had worked early in their careers with Kenyon, and they remembered a woman focused on being a reporter. “She was not a sweet old lady who would stop and mentor you,” he said he was told. “She ate, breathed and slept her job. She was very intrepid and always determined to get the best story. She was always on the lookout for anything that could be a story.” And 100 years ago, she found quite a story in the Scopes Trial. Although she did not get into the courtroom, she was still able to get to the heart of the trial and spectacle in a way that historians and others are still savoring. This article originally appeared on Knoxville News Sentinel: Book celebrates Nellie Kenyon, writer of stories related to Scopes Monkey Trial
